blocks.text: In the third place I count those for whom אנקה anaka is a kind of lizard; they are neither few nor to be despised. For in the Syriac we read ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, which the most learned of the Maronites, Gabriel Sionita ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs], rendered lizard. In the Samaritan [?] semamitha, that is, stellio, as will become clear in its place. In Erpenianus الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, that is, a species of lizard which the barbarous writers call guaril. In the Arabic edited at Paris, الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which is the same thing. [II, 489] For I do not know by what fate it has come about that in Avicenna and others الورك alvvarco is written far more often, although the true spelling is الورل alvvarlo. This is taught by all the Arabic lexicographers, and the barbarous name guaril is derived from it. Not to mention the critical observation found in Damir under the heading ورل [waral] Guaril: لا تلتقي الراء مع اللام الا في اربع مواضع الورل وهو الحيوان المذكور وارل اسم جبل والغرلة وهو القلفة وحرل وهو ضرب من الحجارة [lā taltaqī al-rāʾ maʿa al-lām illā fī arbaʿ mawāḍiʿ al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥayawān al-madhkūr wa-Waral ism jabal wa-al-ghurla wa-huwa al-qulfa wa-ḥaral wa-huwa ḍarb min al-ḥijāra]. Re does not meet with Lam (that is, R with L) except in four places: 1. In alvvarlo, the name of the animal discussed above. 2. In Aral, the name of a mountain, discussed above. 3. In alghorla, which means foreskin (like the Hebrew ערלה). 4. In charal, which is a kind of stone. These, then, are four ancient versions, the Syriac, the Samaritan and the two Arabic, for which anaka is a species of lizard. I have weighty reasons for adding my vote to theirs. 1. Because צב tsab, that is, the land crocodile, came just before, and immediately after are added [col. 1066] four other species of lizards, as will be established from what follows. Hence anaka seems to belong to the same class. For the mygale, or any other animal, would be inserted in a less fitting place amid so many species of lizards. 2. The Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, plainly arose from the Hebrew אנקה anaka. For these two words (apart from the ending, which is Hebrew in the one and Syriac in the other) differ in no respect, except that the Syrians changed the Hebrew NUN into MEM, a change than which nothing is more frequent in those languages. Thus among the Chaldeans or Syrians fortis [strong] is ܚܣܝܢ chasin and ܚܣܝܡ chasim; ratio [reason] ܛܥܢܐ taana and ܛܥܡܐ taama; nympha [nymph] ܢܝܢܦܐ ninphe and ܢܝܡܦܐ nimphe; fustis [club] ܩܘܪܢܣܐ kurnesa and ܩܘܪܡܙܐ kurmeza; the terebinth, or the tree that bears the pistachio, ܒܘܛܡܐ butem, as in Hebrew בוטן boten. And in Arabic the thumb is called ابهام [ibhām] ibham for the Hebrew בהן bohen; so to grow fat, دسم [dasama] dasama, for the Hebrew דשן dasen; and to sing, رنم [ranima] ranima, for the Hebrew רנן ranan. In Ethiopic ዘመወ፡ zamavva, he committed fornication, for the Hebrew ונה zana; እድሜ፡ edem, time, for the Chaldee עדן iddan; አደመ፡ adam, pleasant, sweet, from the Hebrew עדן adan, to delight oneself. Of the same kind is the Egyptian ΜΕΤΩΠΟΝ [metōpon], a kind of ointment, from the Hebrew נטף nataph, or the Chaldee נטופא netopha; ΜΕΙΣΙ [meisi], serpent, from the Hebrew נחש naas. Likewise the Egyptian city Memphis is called by the Prophets now נוף Noph, now מוף Moph. By the same pattern the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha here derives from the Hebrew אנקה anaka, with N and M interchanged. Therefore, whatever the Syriac amaktha is, it is highly probable that the Hebrew anaka is the very same thing. Now it is certain that ܐܡܩܬܐ is a kind of lizard, indeed the stellio, Prov. XXX, 28, where it stands in the Syriac [II, 490] Paraphrase for the Hebrew שממית semamith; just as in the Chaldee, by μετάθεσιν [metathesin] of letters, אקמתא akmetha, which is the same. Therefore, as ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, in Syriac, and אקמתא akmetha in Chaldee is the stellio, so too is the Hebrew אנקה anaka. Hence the Samaritan also renders אנקה anaka by * [?] semamitha, that is, stellio; and both Arabic versions by الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, a kind of lizard close to the stellio, which many therefore take for the stellio, because it is similar in form. Accordingly Alkazuinius says of it: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسوام ابرص [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sawām abraṣ] It is large, of the same form as the guezga and the savvamabras, that is, as the smaller and larger stellios. This is taken from Avicenna. And Alcamus: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh] Alvvarlo (commonly guaril) is an animal like the dhab (or land crocodile). And it is large among those that have the form of the guezga, or stellio. 3. In Hebrew אנקה anaka means a groan and a shrill cry, such as is uttered in great mourning. If anyone denies that the stellio can be so named, as though it were a mute animal, he will be refuted by these words of Pliny on the stellio of Greece, book 29, chapter 4: The Greeks call it colotes, and ascalabotes, and galeotes. It is not born in Italy. For it is full of spots, has a harsh shriek, and * feeds. All of which is foreign to our stellios. Note: a harsh shriek. In Greek you would say τρισμοῦ τραχέος [trismou tracheos], whence it is rightly called אנקה anaka. And as among the Hebrews a masculine plural is often formed from a feminine singular, as [col. 1067] יעלים from יעלה, and יענים from יענה, so from אנקה anaka the plural could be אנקים. And in the second Targum of Esther, chapter 1, verse 2, where among the various animals which each utter their own cry before Solomon are described אנקין בכיין anakin weeping, or wailing, perhaps this should be understood not (as it is commonly taken) of the screaming of eagles, but of the cry and harsh shriek of stellios, which the very word אנקה anaka attests comes close to wailing. And for this very reason the Arabs, knowing at least this much, that the anaka was a kind of lizard, rendered it الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, which itself also has a voice, though perhaps less sonorous. Hence Alcamus: ضغث الورل صوت [ḍaghatha al-waral ṣawt] Dhagathsa alvvarlo, that is, it cried out. This was not sufficiently understood by those of our scholars who have published Arabic Lexicons. For one rendered it The thigh gave a crack, another The hip sounded, because they read الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which means ירך, i. e. hip. But they ought to have remembered that this very الورك occurs everywhere for الورل, as we noted above ^{d)}. Not to mention that in the copy of Alcamus which I used, الورل alvvarlo is correctly written. Therefore, what has hitherto escaped our scholars may be held as [II, 491] established: that in the lizard family some are vocal, and among these is the stellio, which shrieks most shrilly. But we shall say more about the stellio in explaining the word שממית semamith.
